name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Portici

location.address: Parco Superiore della Reggia di Portici (Orto Botanico, University of Naples Federico II), Via Università 100, 80055 Portici

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 07/G902/NA/15

access: Ticketed. The upper park of the Reggia is the University of Naples Federico II's botanical garden; ticket prices and opening hours vary by season, so check with the Centro MUSA visitor centre (081 2532016) before going.
transport: Portici-Via Libertà station on the Circumvesuviana (Naples-Sorrento line) or Portici Bellavista, about 10 minutes' walk to the palace gate on Via Università.
verify_notes: MASAF 400 cm, 18 m. Sources: MASAF only for the tree; the Italian Botanical Heritage page and a Centro MUSA listing confirm the Orto Botanico occupies the upper park of the Reggia. Alive: no dated sighting (iNaturalist empty within 150 m, Commons empty); flagged. Recognise: a fig with buttress roots among the palm and fern areas of the botanical garden, on the east side near the Washingtonia groups registered beside it (sheets 08, 09).
story:
A fig from the rainforests of eastern Australia has made itself at home in the upper park of the Reggia di Portici. Italy's national register of monumental trees measures it at 400 centimetres round the trunk and 18 metres tall.

Moreton Bay figs are built for warm, soft ground. They brace themselves on buttress roots, flat wooden fins that spread out from the base of the trunk, and this one stands among the palm and fern collections of the botanical garden that the University of Naples Federico II keeps in the old royal park. Two groups of Washingtonia palms, also on the national register, stand beside it, so the walk to this corner of the garden takes in three registered entries at once.

The register is the only source that describes this tree on its own. It gives no planting date, and nobody else has published one, so its age is an open question. If you know when it went in, tell us.

We also have no recent dated photograph of it. If you visit and find it standing, a picture from the path would settle that for the next person who comes looking.

The garden is ticketed and its hours change with the season, so check with the University's visitor centre before you take the train out from Naples.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the buttress roots fanning out from a trunk 4 metres round, among the palms and ferns on the east side of the botanical garden next to two groups of Washingtonia palms.

name: The Ginkgo of Portici

location.address: Parco Superiore della Reggia di Portici (Orto Botanico, University of Naples Federico II), Via Università 100, 80055 Portici

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 01/G902/NA/15

access: Ticketed. The upper park of the Reggia is the University of Naples Federico II's botanical garden; ticket prices and opening hours vary by season, so check with the Centro MUSA visitor centre (081 2532016) before going.
transport: Portici-Via Libertà station on the Circumvesuviana (Naples-Sorrento line) or Portici Bellavista, about 10 minutes' walk to the palace gate on Via Università.
verify_notes: MASAF 350 cm, 22 m, the first sheet of Portici. Register only, no dated sighting, flagged. Recognise: the ginkgo in the Parco Superiore; in autumn it turns gold. Camphor ptc_003 stands about 75 m north-east.
story:
When Italy's national register reached Portici, sheet number one went to a ginkgo. It stands 22 metres tall in the upper park of the Reggia, on a trunk 350 centimetres round, and it belongs to a line of trees that was already ancient when the dinosaurs died out.

Ginkgo is the last living species of its family. It reached European gardens from East Asia and has been a fixture of botanical collections ever since, which is exactly where this one lives now, in the botanical garden of the University of Naples Federico II, laid out in the upper park of the old royal palace. A broad camphor tree, also on the register, stands about 75 metres to the north-east, and the two make an easy pair.

For most of the year this is a tall, quiet tree with fan-shaped leaves. Then in autumn the whole crown turns gold, and that is the week to come.

The register does not date it and no other source does either, so how long it has stood here is unknown. If you know, tell us. The register is also the only record of it we have found, with no recent dated photograph, which a single visit would fix.

Entry to the garden is by ticket. Check the hours with the University's visitor centre before you go.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves, gold in autumn, on a crown 22 metres tall, about 75 metres south-west of the broad, low camphor tree in the upper park.

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold

name: The Camphor of Portici

location.address: Parco Superiore della Reggia di Portici (Orto Botanico, University of Naples Federico II), Via Università 100, 80055 Portici

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 02/G902/NA/15

access: Ticketed. The upper park of the Reggia is the University of Naples Federico II's botanical garden; ticket prices and opening hours vary by season, so check with the Centro MUSA visitor centre (081 2532016) before going.
transport: Portici-Via Libertà station on the Circumvesuviana (Naples-Sorrento line) or Portici Bellavista, about 10 minutes' walk to the palace gate on Via Università.
verify_notes: MASAF 420 cm, 12 m (low, wide crown). Register only, flagged. Recognise: broad camphor with glossy leaves and a fissured trunk near the ginkgo ptc_002.
story:
This camphor tree has put its effort into going sideways. Italy's national register gives it a trunk 420 centimetres round, the widest of the trees we map in Portici, and a height of only 12 metres, which makes for a low, broad crown.

The contrast is easy to see on the ground. About 75 metres away stands the registered ginkgo, nearly twice as tall on a thinner trunk. Between them they show two ways an old tree can grow in the same garden.

Camphor trees come from East Asia and keep their glossy leaves all year, and the leaves carry the scent that gave the species its name. This one grows in the botanical garden of the University of Naples Federico II, which occupies the upper park of the Reggia di Portici, the old royal palace on the road from Naples to the Sorrento coast.

The register is the only source that singles it out. It records the size and nothing about when it was planted, and nobody else has dated it, so its age stays a question. If you know, tell us. We have found no recent dated photograph either, so a visitor's picture would be welcome.

The garden charges entry and its hours shift with the seasons. Check with the University's visitor centre before making the trip.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide, low crown of glossy evergreen leaves, only 12 metres tall on a fissured trunk 4.2 metres round, about 75 metres north-east of the ginkgo.

name: The Canary Pine of Portici

location.address: Parco Superiore della Reggia di Portici (Orto Botanico, University of Naples Federico II), Via Università 100, 80055 Portici

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 11/G902/NA/15

access: Not confirmed. The register lists it under the upper park of the Reggia, but its point lies about 700 metres north-east of the botanical garden and whether that corner is open to visitors is unknown; ask the Centro MUSA visitor centre (081 2532016) first.
transport: Portici-Via Libertà station on the Circumvesuviana (Naples-Sorrento line) or Portici Bellavista, about 10 minutes' walk to the palace gate on Via Università.
verify_notes: MASAF 370 cm, 16 m, listed under the Parco Superiore, but its coordinate lies about 700 m north-east of the botanical garden core; whether this corner is open to visitors is unverified. Register only, flagged. Recognise: long drooping needles in threes, thick fire-resistant bark.
story:
Canary pines are built to survive fire. Their bark grows thick enough to shield the living wood when the flames pass, and this one, in the far corner of the old royal park at Portici, carries a trunk 370 centimetres round under a crown 16 metres high, according to Italy's national register of monumental trees.

The species comes from the volcanic islands off north-west Africa and is easy to tell from Italy's own pines. Its needles are long, come in bundles of three and hang down in soft curtains rather than standing stiffly.

There is one thing we cannot tell you yet. The register lists the tree under the upper park of the Reggia, but its point lies about 700 metres north-east of the botanical garden, and we do not know whether that part of the grounds is open to visitors. Ask the University's visitor centre before you set out. If you have walked there, tell us what you found.

The register is also the only source for this tree, with no planting date and no recent dated photograph. Its age is unknown, and anyone who knows it, or who can confirm the tree still stands, would be doing the next visitor a favour by telling us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long drooping needles in bundles of three and very thick bark, in the north-east part of the upper park, about 700 metres from the botanical garden.

name: The Downy Oak of the Lower Park of Portici

location.address: Parco Inferiore della Reggia di Portici, Via Università, 80055 Portici

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 03/G902/NA/15

access: Guided visits only, as far as one listing says; the lower park is only partly open and visitable with a guide. Confirm and book with the Centro MUSA visitor centre (081 2532016), as it is not a free walk-in.
transport: Portici-Via Libertà station on the Circumvesuviana (Naples-Sorrento line) or Portici Bellavista, about 10 minutes' walk to the palace gate on Via Università.
verify_notes: MASAF 310 cm, 28 m (tall for its girth). Register only, flagged; the lower-park access is partial, say so on the page. Recognise: tall oak with grey-green downy leaves in the lower park.
story:
Of the five Portici trees on our map, the tallest is the only one native to southern Italy. This downy oak stands 28 metres high in the lower park of the Reggia, on a trunk 310 centimetres round, according to Italy's national register of monumental trees.

That is tall for an oak of its girth. Downy oaks usually grow broad and knotty on dry hillsides, and their leaves are covered underneath in the fine grey hairs that give the species its name. This one has gone up instead of out.

The neighbours in the upper park are a ginkgo from China, a camphor from East Asia, a fig from Australia and a pine from the Canary Islands. The oak is the tree that would have grown here anyway.

The lower park is a different visit from the botanical garden. A listing describes it as only partly open and visitable with a guide, so plan for a booked visit rather than a walk-in, and confirm with the University's visitor centre first.

The register is the only source for this tree and gives no age. Nobody has published one, and we have no recent dated photograph. If you know when it started, or you see it on a guided walk, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 28 metres on a trunk 3.1 metres round, and the grey-green downy undersides of its leaves, in the lower park rather than the botanical garden.
